title: Electronics II
full_title: Electronic Circuits II: Analog Circuit Design
tagline: Feedback, stability and compensation, op-amp design, output stages, active filters, oscillators and data converters
summary: Building on single transistors and simple stages, this course designs complete analog systems: feedback amplifiers and their stability, the internal design of operational amplifiers, output stages, active filters, oscillators, data converters and the noise that limits them all.
overview: Electronics I taught you to bias a transistor and to treat it as a small-signal amplifier. This course is about what happens when those stages are combined into complete analog systems: an operational amplifier with a gain of a hundred thousand, a power amplifier that drives a loudspeaker, a filter that removes everything above $20\,\mathrm{kHz}$, an oscillator that sets the clock of a radio, a converter that turns a sensor voltage into a stream of bits. These circuits sit at the boundary between the physical world and digital processing, and nearly every electronic product contains several of them.

The unifying idea is **feedback**. A raw amplifier is fast but imprecise: its gain depends on temperature, supply voltage and the spread of transistor parameters. Wrapping it in a loop of accurate passive components trades surplus gain for precision, linearity and controlled impedances. The same loop that makes an amplifier precise can also make it oscillate, so the second chapter studies stability and frequency compensation with the tools of Bode and Nyquist. The course then opens the op-amp to see how its stages are designed, adds output stages that deliver power efficiently, and applies feedback deliberately to build active filters and oscillators.

The last two chapters face the limits of analog design. Data converters must resolve a voltage to one part in $2^N$, which turns small errors such as offset, mismatch and settling into first-order concerns; and every signal must compete with the **noise** generated by the resistors and transistors themselves. Analog design is hard because many specifications conflict — gain against bandwidth, speed against power, noise against area — and few problems have a single right answer. Work every example with real numbers, check orders of magnitude, and keep asking which approximation you are making and when it fails.
outcomes: Analyse a feedback amplifier by identifying its topology, loop gain and feedback factor, and predict its closed-loop gain, bandwidth and input and output impedances.
Assess the stability of a feedback amplifier from its loop gain using poles, gain margin and phase margin, and relate phase margin to step-response overshoot.
Design dominant-pole and Miller compensation for a two-stage amplifier to meet a phase-margin and unity-gain-frequency specification.
Analyse and size a two-stage CMOS operational amplifier, computing its gain, slew rate, offset, common-mode range and output swing.
Compare class A, B and AB output stages in terms of efficiency, crossover distortion and power dissipation, and choose a heat sink for a given power device.
Design Butterworth and Chebyshev active filters with Sallen–Key and biquad sections, and explain the operation of switched-capacitor filters.
Derive the oscillation condition for RC, LC and crystal oscillators from the Barkhausen criterion, and explain amplitude stabilisation and relaxation oscillators.
Explain sampling, quantisation and the main DAC and ADC architectures, and compute resolution, quantisation noise and signal-to-noise ratio.
Model thermal, shot and flicker noise in resistors, transistors and amplifiers, compute input-referred noise and noise figure, and apply low-noise design principles.

chapters.title: Feedback
chapters.summary: Negative feedback, loop gain, the four feedback topologies and their effect on gain, bandwidth and impedances.

chapters.title: Stability and frequency compensation
chapters.summary: Poles of feedback amplifiers, gain and phase margins, and dominant-pole and Miller compensation.

chapters.title: Operational amplifier design
chapters.summary: Two-stage CMOS and bipolar op-amps, specifications, slew rate, offset and common-mode range.

chapters.title: Output stages and power amplifiers
chapters.summary: Class A, B and AB output stages, efficiency, distortion and thermal considerations.

chapters.title: Active filter design
chapters.summary: Butterworth and Chebyshev approximations, Sallen–Key and biquad realisations, and switched-capacitor filters.

chapters.title: Oscillators
chapters.summary: The Barkhausen criterion, RC, LC and crystal oscillators, amplitude stabilisation and relaxation oscillators.

chapters.title: Data converters
chapters.summary: Sample-and-hold circuits, quantisation, DAC architectures, and flash, successive-approximation and sigma–delta ADCs.

chapters.title: Noise in electronic circuits
chapters.summary: Thermal, shot and flicker noise, noise models of devices and amplifiers, noise figure and low-noise design.

history.title: Shot noise explained
history.detail: Walter Schottky showed that the discreteness of electronic charge produces a current fluctuation with a flat spectrum proportional to the mean current, now written $2qI$.

history.title: The quartz crystal oscillator
history.detail: Walter Cady used a piezoelectric quartz resonator to control the frequency of a valve oscillator, the ancestor of every crystal clock.

history.title: The negative-feedback amplifier
history.detail: Harold Black conceived the negative-feedback amplifier to linearise telephone repeaters; his patent was filed in 1928 and his paper 'Stabilized feedback amplifiers' appeared in 1934.

history.title: Thermal noise measured and explained
history.detail: John B. Johnson measured the noise voltage of resistors, and Harry Nyquist derived its value $4kTR$ per unit bandwidth from thermodynamics, in back-to-back papers in Physical Review.

history.title: The Nyquist stability criterion
history.detail: In 'Regeneration theory' Nyquist showed how to decide the stability of a feedback amplifier from its measured loop frequency response.

history.title: The Wien-bridge oscillator
history.detail: William Hewlett's Stanford thesis described a Wien-bridge audio oscillator whose amplitude was stabilised by a lamp; it became the HP 200A, Hewlett-Packard's first product.

history.title: Bode's feedback amplifier design
history.detail: Hendrik Bode's book 'Network Analysis and Feedback Amplifier Design' set out gain and phase margins and the gain–phase relations used to compensate amplifiers.

history.title: Delta–sigma modulation
history.detail: Hiroshi Inose, Yasuhiko Yasuda and Jun Murakami described delta–sigma modulation, the basis of the oversampling converters in almost every audio system today.

history.title: The μA741
history.detail: Fairchild's μA741, designed by David Fullagar, put a 30 pF Miller compensation capacitor on the chip and made the internally compensated op-amp the industry standard.

references.title: Microelectronic Circuits (8th ed.)
references.authors: Adel S. Sedra, Kenneth C. Smith, Tony Chan Carusone, Vincent Gaudet
references.note: The standard undergraduate text; its chapters on feedback, output stages, filters, oscillators and op-amp internals follow the same order as this course.

references.title: Design of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits (2nd ed.)
references.note: Clear, intuitive treatment of CMOS op-amp design, stability and compensation, and noise; the best next step for integrated-circuit design.

references.title: Analysis and Design of Analog Integrated Circuits (5th ed.)
references.authors: Paul R. Gray, Paul J. Hurst, Stephen H. Lewis, Robert G. Meyer
references.note: The authoritative reference on bipolar and CMOS amplifiers, output stages, feedback, frequency response and noise, with careful derivations.

references.title: Analog Integrated Circuit Design (2nd ed.)
references.authors: Tony Chan Carusone, David A. Johns, Kenneth W. Martin
references.note: Strong on switched-capacitor circuits, continuous-time filters, data converters and oversampling.

references.title: The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)
references.note: Practical wisdom on real op-amps, power stages, oscillators, converters and low-noise design, with many measured examples.

references.title: Design with Operational Amplifiers and Analog Integrated Circuits (4th ed.)
references.note: Op-amp applications from the user's side: active filters, stability, noise, oscillators and data converters, with worked designs.

references.title: Design of Analog Filters (2nd ed.)
references.authors: Rolf Schaumann, Haiqiao Xiao, Mac E. Van Valkenburg
references.note: Approximation theory, sensitivity and active-RC, biquad and switched-capacitor realisations in depth.
